cards.front: In a circulation at steady state, what equation links the mean pressure drop across a circuit to its flow and resistance?
cards.back: Pressure drop = flow × resistance.
cards.why: At a given flow, a circuit that is harder to push through costs more pressure, as water needs more push through a narrow pipe than a wide one.
cards.quote: just as water needs more push through a narrow pipe than a wide one: pressure drop = flow × resistance.

cards.front: Is pressure drop = flow × resistance a statement about how the body controls blood flow?
cards.back: No. It is bookkeeping for beat-averaged pressures in a steady state. In a living body the heart and vessels set the flow together, and changing a resistance can change the flow.
cards.quote: The rule is bookkeeping, not a claim about control: in a living body the heart and vessels set the flow together, and changing a resistance can change the flow.

cards.front: Why does a large animal need bulk flow rather than diffusion alone to supply its tissues?
cards.back: Diffusion is quick over micrometres but far too slow over centimetres. A pump drives the whole fluid, and diffusion does only the last short step.
cards.quote: so a large animal relies on bulk flow: a pump drives the whole fluid, and diffusion does only the last short step.
cards.section: Bulk flow, open and closed

cards.front: How does a closed circulatory system differ from an open one in where the fluid goes and where exchange happens?
cards.back: Closed: blood stays inside vessels, and exchange happens across thin capillary walls. Open: the fluid leaves the vessels and bathes the organs directly in body spaces, the hemocoel.
cards.quote: In a closed circulatory system, blood stays inside vessels, and exchange happens across the thin walls of capillaries, the smallest vessels.
cards.section: Bulk flow, open and closed

cards.front: In an open circulatory system, the circulating fluid, called {{c1::hemolymph}}, leaves the vessels and flows through the hemocoel, body spaces that bathe the organs directly.
cards.back: It is blood and tissue fluid in one.
cards.quote: the fluid, called hemolymph because it is blood and tissue fluid in one, leaves the vessels and flows through the hemocoel
cards.section: Bulk flow, open and closed

cards.front: Classify each animal's circulation as open or closed: grasshopper, snail, earthworm, squid, trout.
cards.back: Open: grasshopper, snail. Closed: earthworm, squid, trout.
cards.why: Open and closed do not split invertebrates from vertebrates. Earthworms have muscular pumping vessels; squid are molluscs with closed circulation; all vertebrates are closed.
cards.quote: Open and closed do not split invertebrates from vertebrates.
cards.section: Bulk flow, open and closed

cards.front: Squid and octopuses have closed circulation, with two {{c1::branchial hearts}} that push blood through the gills and a systemic heart that sends it to the body.
cards.quote: Squid and octopuses, which are molluscs, are closed too, with two branchial hearts that push blood through the gills and a systemic heart that sends it to the body.
cards.section: Bulk flow, open and closed

cards.front: What makes a vessel an artery or a vein?
cards.back: Direction, not oxygen content. An artery carries blood away from the heart; a vein carries it toward the heart.
cards.quote: An artery carries blood away from the heart and a vein carries it toward the heart, whatever its oxygen content.
cards.section: Through the mammalian heart, valve by valve

cards.front: Trace blood through the mammalian heart after birth, from the venae cavae to the aorta, naming each chamber and valve.
cards.back: Venae cavae → right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonary valve → pulmonary trunk and arteries → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → mitral valve → left ventricle → aortic valve → aorta.
cards.quote: The left ventricle pushes it through the aortic valve into the aorta, and on to the body.
cards.section: Through the mammalian heart, valve by valve

cards.front: What makes a heart valve open or close?
cards.back: Pressure alone. It opens when pressure behind it exceeds pressure ahead, and closes when that reverses.
cards.quote: Each valve is a one-way door: it opens when pressure behind it exceeds pressure ahead, and closes when that reverses.
cards.section: Through the mammalian heart, valve by valve

cards.front: Name, in order, the four phases of one beat of the adult human left ventricle.
cards.back: Filling (diastole), isovolumic contraction (systole), ejection (systole), isovolumic relaxation (diastole).
cards.quote: For the adult human left ventricle at rest, one beat has four phases (pressures in mmHg, millimetres of mercury):
cards.section: Through the mammalian heart, valve by valve

cards.front: In the adult human left ventricle, why is the start of contraction isovolumic?
cards.back: Ventricular pressure is above atrial pressure, so the mitral valve shuts, but still below aortic pressure, so the aortic valve stays shut. With both shut, volume cannot change.
cards.quote: Ventricle above atrium, so the mitral valve shuts; still below the aorta, so the aortic valve stays shut.
cards.section: Through the mammalian heart, valve by valve

cards.front: At one instant in an adult human left ventricle, ventricular pressure is 40 mmHg and falling, left atrial pressure is about 8 mmHg, and aortic pressure is about 90 mmHg. Which valves are open, and which phase is this?
cards.back: Neither valve is open: isovolumic relaxation.
cards.why: The ventricle is below the aorta, so the aortic valve is shut, and above the atrium, so the mitral valve stays shut until ventricular pressure drops below atrial pressure.
cards.quote: Ventricle falls below the aorta, so the aortic valve shuts; both stay shut until ventricular pressure drops below atrial pressure and the mitral valve opens again.
cards.section: Through the mammalian heart, valve by valve

cards.front: In a resting adult human blood pressure of "120 over 80 mmHg", whose pressure is the 80?
cards.back: The aorta's lowest pressure, not the ventricle's. Left ventricular pressure falls to a few mmHg as it fills.
cards.why: The aortic valve shuts when the ventricle falls below the aorta, so the aorta holds its pressure between beats.
cards.quote: So in "120 over 80 mmHg", the 80 is the aorta's lowest pressure, not the ventricle's, which falls to a few mmHg as it fills.
cards.section: Through the mammalian heart, valve by valve

cards.front: In a resting adult human, the left ventricle peaks near 120 mmHg and the right near 25 mmHg at the same flow. Why is 120 / 25 the wrong estimate of how much more resistance the body circuit has than the lung circuit?
cards.back: Resistance is the mean (beat-averaged) pressure drop divided by flow, not a ratio of peak pressures. Using mean drops, the body circuit's resistance is about 15 times the lungs', not 5.
cards.quote: Resistance is the mean (beat-averaged) pressure drop divided by flow, not a ratio of peaks:
cards.section: Through the mammalian heart, valve by valve

cards.front: Illustrative resting adult human: each ventricle pumps about 5 L per min. Mean pressure is about 93 mmHg entering the body circuit and 3 mmHg leaving it, about 14 mmHg entering the lung circuit and 8 mmHg leaving it. Find each circuit's resistance.
cards.back: Body: (93 - 3) / 5 = 90 / 5 = 18 mmHg per L per min. Lungs: (14 - 8) / 5 = 6 / 5 = 1.2 mmHg per L per min. Body / lungs = 18 / 1.2 = 15.
cards.quote: about 90 / 5 = 18 for the body against 6 / 5 = 1.2 for the lungs (table), about 15 times as much.
cards.section: Through the mammalian heart, valve by valve

cards.front: An illustrative human body circuit has a resistance of 18 mmHg per L per min. If flow were 6 L per min with resistance unchanged, what mean pressure drop would the bookkeeping rule require across the body circuit?
cards.back: Pressure drop = flow × resistance = 6 L per min × 18 mmHg per L per min = 108 mmHg.
cards.why: The rule is bookkeeping: in a living body a change in flow can come with a change in resistance.
cards.quote: At a given flow, the pressure a circuit costs depends on how hard it is to push through, its resistance,

cards.front: What distinguishes single circulation from double circulation?
cards.back: In single circulation blood passes through the heart once per loop. In double circulation it passes twice: once on a pulmonary circuit to the gas-exchange organ, once on a systemic circuit to the body.
cards.quote: In single circulation, blood passes through the heart once per loop; in double circulation, twice:
cards.section: One circuit or two

cards.front: A teleost fish and a mammal each need to perfuse the body. Why must the teleost supply its body at lower pressure than its ventricle makes, while a mammal's left ventricle can drive the body circuit directly?
cards.back: In the teleost, one ventricle drives blood through the gill capillaries and then on to the body, so pressure is spent across the gills first. In a mammal, the four chambers keep the circuits separate, each with its own pump, so no gas-exchange capillary bed sits in series ahead of the body circuit, and the left ventricle drives it directly.
cards.why: Pressure drop = flow × resistance: the gill capillaries in series take their drop before the body gets any.
cards.quote: Birds and mammals have four chambers that keep the circuits fully separate, each with its own pump.
cards.section: One circuit or two

cards.front: A frog heart has two atria and one ventricle. Why does its right atrium receive some oxygen-rich blood?
cards.back: Frog skin exchanges gas, so oxygen-rich blood from the skin returns with the body blood to the right atrium. The ventricle feeds a pulmocutaneous circuit (lungs and skin) and a systemic circuit.
cards.quote: The right atrium receives body blood, including oxygen-rich blood from the skin; the left receives lung blood.
cards.section: One circuit or two

cards.front: In a crocodilian heart, the right ventricle opens into both the pulmonary artery and the left aorta. Why does the left aortic valve usually stay shut?
cards.back: The foramen of Panizza joins the left aorta to the right aorta, which the left ventricle fills at body pressure. So the left aorta usually holds more pressure than the right ventricle makes.
cards.quote: So the left aorta usually holds more pressure than the right ventricle makes, keeping the left aortic valve shut.
cards.section: One circuit or two

cards.front: In a crocodilian, resistance to flow into the lungs rises. Where can right-ventricle blood go, and why?
cards.back: Part of it leaves by the left aorta, bypassing the lungs: a shunt.
cards.why: Right ventricular pressure climbs until it passes left-aortic pressure, and the left aortic valve then opens.
cards.quote: the left aortic valve then opens and part of the output leaves by the left aorta, bypassing the lungs: a shunt.
cards.section: One circuit or two

cards.front: A crocodilian actively closes down its cog-tooth valve. Using the valve rule and pressure drop = flow × resistance, predict what happens to right ventricular pressure and to the route of its output.
cards.back: Right ventricular pressure rises toward the shunt threshold. Once it passes left-aortic pressure, the left aortic valve opens and part of the output bypasses the lungs through the left aorta.
cards.why: The cog-tooth valve's nodules restrict flow to the lungs, raising resistance; a valve opens when pressure behind it exceeds pressure ahead.
cards.quote: Connective-tissue nodules in the right ventricle's pulmonary outflow tract, the cog-tooth valve, move under active control and restrict flow to the lungs
cards.section: The crocodile shunt can be driven

cards.front: Are frog and crocodile hearts imperfect steps toward the mammalian four-chambered heart?
cards.back: No. A frog heart that sends blood to the skin, or a crocodile heart that bypasses the lungs, works well in its own animal. Birds and mammals also reached four chambers independently.
cards.quote: None of these hearts is a step toward the mammal's:
cards.section: One circuit or two

cards.front: Stroke volume = {{c1::EDV - ESV}} (end-diastolic volume minus end-systolic volume).
cards.quote: stroke volume = EDV - ESV and cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume
cards.section: Harvey's numbers, redone

cards.front: Illustrative resting adult human left ventricle: heart rate 80 beats per min, end-diastolic volume 125 mL, end-systolic volume 55 mL. Find stroke volume, cardiac output and ejection fraction.
cards.back: Stroke volume = 125 - 55 = 70 mL. Cardiac output = 80 × 70 = 5,600 mL per min = 5.6 L per min. Ejection fraction = 70 / 125 = 0.56, or 56 percent.
cards.quote: stroke volume = EDV - ESV and cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume and ejection fraction = stroke volume / EDV
cards.section: Harvey's numbers, redone

cards.front: The left ventricle of a resting human pumps about 5.25 L per min. Why is the heart's total output not 10.5 L per min?
cards.back: The two ventricles pump in series, the same blood passing through one and then the other, so their outputs are not added.
cards.quote: for one ventricle; the two pump in series, so their outputs are not added.
cards.section: Harvey's numbers, redone

cards.front: Illustrative resting human: heart rate 60 beats per min, stroke volume 70 mL, 5.0 L of blood. How long, on average, does a volume equal to all the blood take to pass one side of the heart, and how much does that side pump in an hour?
cards.back: Cardiac output = 60 × 70 = 4,200 mL per min = 4.2 L per min. Turnover = 5.0 / 4.2 = 1.19 min, about 71 s. In an hour, 4.2 × 60 = 252 L, about 50 times the body's blood.
cards.why: This is an average turnover time; some blood takes short routes and some longer ones.
cards.quote: A volume equal to all of it passes through one side of the heart in 5.0 / 5.25 = 0.95 min, about 57 seconds.
cards.section: Harvey's numbers, redone

cards.front: Someone claims blood pumped by the heart is used up in the tissues and replaced with new blood. Using cardiac output arithmetic for a resting human (5.25 L per min, 5.0 L of blood), refute it, even allowing stroke volume to be half your estimate.
cards.back: One side pumps 5.25 × 30 = 157.5 L in half an hour, more than 30 times the body's blood. Halving stroke volume still gives about 79 L, nearly 16 times. So the same blood must go round.
cards.why: Cardiac output × time compared with total blood volume is Harvey's argument.
cards.quote: In half an hour that side pumps 5.25 x 30 = 157.5 L, more than 30 times the body's blood;
cards.section: Harvey's numbers, redone

cards.front: Harvey pressed along a vein. What did this show about the direction of venous flow, and what could his argument not show?
cards.back: The vein's valves pass blood only toward the heart. His argument did not show how arteries connect to veins; capillaries were seen later, by Malpighi in the frog lung.
cards.quote: Harvey pressed along a vein to show that its valves pass blood only toward the heart.
cards.section: Harvey's numbers, redone

cards.front: In a healthy mammalian heart, what sets the heart rate?
cards.back: The sinoatrial (SA) node. Its cells drift slowly up to threshold, fire, and start again; that drift, the prepotential, sets the rate.
cards.quote: Its cells drift slowly upward in voltage to the threshold for an impulse, fire, and start again; that drift, the prepotential, sets the heart rate.
cards.section: The rate dial: pacemaker and conduction

cards.front: Give the path of excitation through the mammalian heart, from the SA node to the ventricle walls.
cards.back: SA node → both atria → atrioventricular (AV) node, where conduction slows → bundle of His → right and left bundle branches → Purkinje fibres in the ventricle walls.
cards.quote: Excitation then runs down the bundle of His, its right and left branches, and the Purkinje fibres in the ventricle walls.
cards.section: The rate dial: pacemaker and conduction

cards.front: Why does conduction slow at the atrioventricular (AV) node?
cards.back: The delay lets the atria finish contracting before the ventricles start, so the atria's push, the last part of filling, comes in time.
cards.quote: The delay lets the atria finish contracting before the ventricles start.
cards.section: The rate dial: pacemaker and conduction

cards.front: Predict the change in heart rate in each case: (a) the vagus nerve is stimulated; (b) sympathetic nerves to the heart are stimulated; (c) adrenaline rises in the blood.
cards.back: (a) Rate falls. (b) Rate rises. (c) Rate rises.
cards.why: Sympathetic input speeds the SA node, the parasympathetic vagus slows it, and circulating adrenaline raises the rate.
cards.quote: sympathetic speeds the SA node, the parasympathetic vagus slows it), circulating adrenaline raises the rate.
cards.section: The rate dial: pacemaker and conduction

cards.front: Suppose the AV node delay were abolished, so atria and ventricles contracted almost together, with heart rate and contractility unchanged. Predict the effect on ventricular filling, stroke volume and cardiac output.
cards.back: The atria's push would come too late, so filling is expected to be less complete; by Frank-Starling that lowers stroke volume, and cardiac output with it.
cards.why: The atria's push, the last part of filling, would come too late; by the Frank-Starling relation less filling gives a smaller stroke volume; output = rate × stroke volume.
cards.quote: Without it the two would contract almost together, and the atria's push, the last part of filling, would come too late.
cards.section: The rate dial: pacemaker and conduction

cards.front: In Starling's dog heart-lung preparation, the heart is cut off from its nerves and a reservoir sets venous return. Raising the reservoir makes the heart fill further and its output rise. What does the absence of nerves let you conclude?
cards.back: The rise in output with filling comes from the heart itself, not from nervous control.
cards.quote: With nerves removed, the change came from the heart itself.
cards.section: The stroke volume dial: filling, contractility and load

cards.front: What is preload?
cards.back: How much the ventricle is filled and stretched before it contracts.
cards.quote: Preload is how much the ventricle is filled and stretched before it contracts.
cards.section: The stroke volume dial: filling, contractility and load

cards.front: {{c1::Afterload}} is the pressure the ventricle ejects against; vessel resistance helps set it.
cards.quote: The third input, afterload, is the pressure the ventricle ejects against; vessel resistance helps set it
cards.section: The stroke volume dial: filling, contractility and load

cards.front: How do more filling and sympathetic stimulation differ in their effect on the Frank-Starling curve of stroke volume against end-diastolic volume?
cards.back: More filling moves the heart along the curve to a larger stroke volume. Sympathetic stimulation raises contractility, the strength of contraction at a given filling, and lifts the whole curve.
cards.quote: Sympathetic stimulation raises contractility, the strength of contraction at a given filling, and so lifts the whole curve.
cards.section: The stroke volume dial: filling, contractility and load

cards.front: After moderate blood loss in an adult human at rest, less blood returns to the heart and the ventricles fill less. If heart rate and contractility did not change, what would happen to stroke volume and cardiac output?
cards.back: Both fall.
cards.why: By the Frank-Starling relation, lower end-diastolic volume gives a smaller stroke volume; cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume.
cards.quote: By the Frank-Starling relation, over the normal range stroke volume rises along a curve as end-diastolic volume rises.
cards.section: The stroke volume dial: filling, contractility and load

cards.front: Sympathetic stimulation of the heart at unchanged filling: predict the change in cardiac output, naming both dials it turns.
cards.back: Cardiac output rises through both factors: heart rate rises (sympathetic speeds the SA node) and stroke volume rises (higher contractility lifts the Frank-Starling curve).
cards.why: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume, so raising both multiplies the effect.
cards.quote: cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume and ejection fraction = stroke volume / EDV
cards.section: Harvey's numbers, redone

cards.front: In conscious pythons, mean arterial pressure was 75.7 cm H2O systemic and 11.6 cm H2O pulmonary. Convert to mmHg (1 mmHg = 1.36 cm H2O) and give the ratio.
cards.back: 75.7 / 1.36 = 55.7 mmHg; 11.6 / 1.36 = 8.5 mmHg. Ratio 75.7 / 11.6 = 6.5, the same in either unit.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A python's single ventricle supplies systemic arteries at a much higher mean pressure than the pulmonary artery. Design a measurement to test whether the ventricle works as two regions during contraction, and say what it cannot rule out.
cards.back: Record pressure in both regions of the ventricle at once through the beat; separate systolic peaks support functional division. Separate pressures do not rule out some mixing of blood, so measure that separately.
cards.why: A gap in mean pressure alone could come from how the two sets of arteries drain between beats; one open chamber would give the same peak to both outflows.
cards.quote: To test it, record pressure in both regions at once through the beat: separate systolic peaks support functional division.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In a teleost fish, what does the bulbus arteriosus do, and why does it matter?
cards.back: It is an elastic outflow, rich in smooth muscle, that receives the ventricle's ejection. Its low stiffness damps pressure swings before the delicate gill capillaries.
cards.quote: Its low stiffness damps pressure swings before the delicate gill capillaries
cards.section: Fish chambers and the bird-mammal split
